timeline.title: Trying More on My Own
paragraphs: I started building projects that combined code, sensors, and movement. An Arduino car taught me how to work with motors and sensors, and later I discovered the ESP32 and built a simple web page that let me control servos from my phone.

This was also when I started moving away from copying tutorials and trying more ideas of my own. By the end of 7th grade, I signed up for PLTW Introduction to Engineering because I wanted to learn more before taking on bigger projects.

timeline.title: The Spark
paragraphs: My dad gave me an Arduino Starter Kit for my birthday. I started with a blinking LED, then buttons, sensors, and projects I found online. Most of them did not work the first time, but I loved seeing a few lines of code make something happen in the real world.

timeline.title: Gears Before Code
paragraphs: I spent a lot of time building LEGO and other mechanical sets with motors, gears, and moving parts. I liked following the instructions at first, but I liked taking things apart and changing them even more.
By the end of 5th grade, I wanted to do more than connect gears and motors. I wanted to control what I built with code.

AERO-LITE: I want to continue testing the project and collect better data to understand how well the CO₂ capture idea actually works.
Aerospace: I want to take on bigger aerospace and rocketry projects that push me to learn more physics, engineering, teamwork, and testing.

Keep Building: As I learn more math, science, programming, and engineering, I want my projects to grow with me. I hope I keep choosing things that are just a little beyond what I already know how to do.

beliefs.title: Start Small
beliefs.text: Big projects feel less overwhelming when I start with one simple goal. Make one motor move. Read one sensor. Get one part working. Then build from there.

beliefs.title: Test, Don't Guess
beliefs.text: When something does not work, I try to change one thing at a time and see what actually happens. I have learned that guessing usually creates more problems.

beliefs.title: Learn From What Breaks
beliefs.text: I have burned boards, wired things incorrectly, and spent hours chasing the wrong problem. Those mistakes are frustrating, but they are also the parts I usually remember and learn from the most.

beliefs.title: Keep It Simple
beliefs.text: I used to think adding more parts and features made a project better. Now I try to find the simplest solution that does the job well before making it more complicated.

beliefs.title: Build Safely
beliefs.text: Working with batteries, motors, heat, and moving parts has taught me to think about what could go wrong before I turn something on. A working project is not worth much if it is not safe.

beliefs.title: Share What I Learn
beliefs.text: I document my projects because I know how helpful it is to find someone else's explanation when I am stuck. If my notes help another student get past a problem, they are worth writing.

problem_cards.title: ISS Solution: CDRA

problem_cards.title: AERO-LITE
lines: Early prototype: zeolite, silica gel, sensors, and dashboard.
problem_cards.win: Goal: capture, release, and reuse the sorbent. Full-cycle performance still needs testing.

stages.title: DRY
stages.text: Silica gel strips moisture from cabin air. Humidity kills CO₂ capture efficiency, so this happens first.

stages.title: TRAP
stages.text: Zeolite 13X bed captures CO₂ at room temperature. Nitrogen and oxygen pass through. Clean air returns to the cabin.

stages.title: RELEASE
stages.text: Planned regeneration stage: use controlled heating to release CO₂ adsorbed on the zeolite. The first prototype simulated heater control; repeatable regeneration and resulting CO₂ concentration still need to be tested.

stages.title: COMPRESS
stages.text: Planned downstream stage: compress a CO₂-rich stream into a buffer tank for possible use with a Sabatier system. The compressor, pressure target, and continuous-feed integration require future validation.

aero_lite.cycle_note: Intended control schedule: ADSORB (~5 min) → REGEN (~1 min) → PURGE (~15 sec), totaling ~6 min 15 sec. This is a design setting, not a validated full regeneration-cycle measurement. The proposed buffer tank is intended to smooth the intermittent output for downstream use; that integration remains to be tested.
aero_lite.prototype_text: This is not a rendering. It is three mason jars on my desk, a live ESP32-S3, and a web dashboard that updates every second.
prototype_bullets: Stage 1: Silica gel beads (orange, indicating type)
Stage 2+3: Zeolite 13X pellets in a shared bed
Stage 4: CO₂ buffer tank with pressure sensor
Control: ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1 with TCA9548A multiplexer
Dashboard: Pure HTML/CSS/JS, polling JSON API at 1 Hz
aero_lite.prototype_data: One recorded dashboard snapshot: Cabin sensor 1,029 ppm; Purified sensor 477 ppm. These readings illustrate the prototype sensor output, not validated CO₂ capture efficiency or sustained performance.

learnings.title: 💡 Capture First, Compress Later
learnings.text: I initially thought compressing cabin air could give me a useful CO₂ stream. Then I realized compression alone does not separate the gases. I redesigned the concept to capture CO₂ before any downstream compression. Actual power and mass savings still need testing.

learnings.title: 🔥 Thermal Swing > Pressure Swing
learnings.text: Pressure swing uses less energy, but vacuum seals in microgravity are catastrophic leak risks. A PTC heater with a bimetallic cutoff is safer — even if the ESP32 crashes.

learnings.title: 📊 The Dashboard Is Evidence, Not an Efficiency Test
learnings.text: Real hardware and live sensor readings made the project concrete. One dashboard snapshot did not establish capture efficiency; I need repeatable experiments and controlled measurements for that.

aero_lite.repo_text: All firmware, schematics, 3D models, and documentation are open source.

hero.headline: How could astronauts manage CO₂ on the Moon?
hero.thesis: A regenerative CO₂ preprocessor concept for future lunar habitats — prototyped by an 8th grader on his desk.
hero.intro: I started AERO-LITE in mid-March 2026 after an email from Space Center Houston described a Carbon Capture Challenge. I had learned a little about electronics and robotics before this, but almost nothing about air chemistry. I decided to learn it the way I usually do: by building something real and seeing what it can actually prove.

question.heading: Why was a lunar habitat an interesting place to think about air?
paragraphs: Space Center Houston's Carbon Capture Challenge asked students to think about how future Moon habitats would manage the CO₂ that people exhale — with limited power and mass. That constraint is what pulled me in: on Earth, fresh air solves most buildings' CO₂ problems. In a sealed habitat, you have to decide where the CO₂ actually goes.

The station-grade answer today is a big machine that vents CO₂ overboard. And everything I read about keeping people alive in a surface habitat comes back to the same idea: the air will be recycled, so each part of the system — capture, release, storage — becomes part of a loop, not a one-way stream.

I am not going to pretend an 8th grader solved habitat engineering. What I had was a question from people who run a real space center, three months to try something, and a habit: when I don't understand something, prototype it small and see what the numbers say.

decision.heading: The calculation that changed AERO-LITE
decision.intro: My first concept looked elegantly simple: pull cabin air into a compressor, squeeze it, get a concentrated CO₂ stream. One stage instead of several. Less mass, fewer parts. I liked it so much I started sketching the compressor placement before doing the arithmetic.
decision.key_heading: Cabin air is mostly not CO₂ — so compressing it compresses mostly everything else.
paragraphs: Cabin air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Squeezing it does not separate the components; it just makes harder-to-manage mixed gas. When I sat down with the composition, the "one elegant stage" stopped looking elegant — it would spend the project's energy on ~99% of the air that isn't CO₂.

So AERO-LITE reversed direction: capture CO₂ first, then — later in the design — compress a stream that is actually CO₂-rich. That single decision is why the prototype is a sorbent bed with sensors, not a compressor with plexiglass. The power and mass savings the redesign promises are estimates; testing them is exactly the work I have listed as unfinished.

process.heading: Four stages — two on the bench, two on paper
process.intro: The concept is a four-stage loop. Honesty check before anything else: the first two stages exist as real hardware. The last two are design stages — the concept for them exists, the hardware outcome does not.

stages.title: DRY
stages.text: Silica gel strips moisture first — humidity kills CO₂ capture efficiency, so this stage has to come first.

stages.title: TRAP
stages.text: A zeolite 13X bed captures CO₂ at room temperature; nitrogen and oxygen pass through. Three live sensors watch the result.

stages.title: RELEASE
stages.text: Controlled heating would release the captured CO₂ for reuse. The first prototype only simulated heater control.

stages.title: COMPRESS
stages.text: A CO₂-rich stream would be compressed into a buffer tank for possible downstream use. Not built, not integrated.

process.cycle_note: Intended control schedule: ADSORB (~5 min) → REGEN (~1 min) → PURGE (~15 s), about 6 minutes 15 seconds total.
process.cycle_verdict: This is a design setting, not a validated full regeneration-cycle measurement.
process.cycle_note_more: The buffer tank idea is meant to smooth the intermittent output; that integration still needs to be tested.

spec_rows.value: CO₂ buffer tank with pressure sensor (concepted)

evidence.heading: What the prototype actually shows
evidence.intro: I wanted the first build to be the least impressive possible version of the idea: jars, beads, sensors — not a rendering, not a sci-fi panel. A bench prototype can tell you whether a component behaves; it cannot yet tell you whether the whole loop is efficient.
evidence.photo_alt: AERO-LITE Phase 1 prototype — three mason jars with zeolite beads, silica gel, and CO₂ sensors on a desk
evidence.photo_caption: Three mason jars: silica gel, zeolite 13X, and a buffer-tank stand-in — with the live sensors between them.
evidence.observed_lead_text: cabin sensor 1,029 ppm; purified sensor 477 ppm.
observed_paragraphs: These readings illustrate live sensor output from real hardware. A single snapshot does not establish capture efficiency or sustained performance.
Reliable across the three sensors — including the I²C channel selection behind them — took its own debugging story.
evidence.missing_asset_text: The CO₂ dashboard is real, not a mockup — a web UI served by the ESP32-S3 that updates every second. The readings shown under OBSERVED above were captured from it as live sensor output; this page describes it through those readings and the bench photograph rather than a stylized UI frame.
evidence.pull_quote: This is not a rendering. It is three mason jars on my desk, a live ESP32-S3, and a web dashboard that updates every second.

lessons.heading: What fought back — and what I'd test next
lessons.intro: The hard parts weren't the ones I predicted. None of these lessons would have appeared in a slideshow; they only showed up at the bench.

items.title: Compression is not separation
items.text: My original design rested on a mistake I didn't notice until I checked the composition of air. Squeezing mixed gas doesn't sort it. Catching this early cost me a week of sketches and saved the whole project — the numbers proved it, so I redesigned before building.

items.title: Three sensors that wouldn't answer
items.text: The three SCD41 sensors sat behind an I²C multiplexer and kept going silent. The channel-mask math was right, but the code didn't always select the right channel before each read. Three days of testing assumptions one at a time fixed it — and I now write the intended channel selection right before every sensor communication.

items.title: Heat beats vacuum — for now
items.text: For releasing CO₂ from the zeolite, a pressure-swing approach would use less energy. But vacuum seals on moving hardware in rough conditions are leak risks. A PTC heater with a bimetallic cutoff is the safer path for this prototype — even if the microcontroller crashed, the cutoff would remain. That trade-off is a design decision, not a proven result.

items.title: A dashboard is evidence, not a verdict
items.text: Live readings made the project feel real — and I had to learn not to oversell them. One clean-looking number is a snapshot, not an efficiency measurement. Explaining that distinction to judges taught me as much as building it did.

lessons.next_steps: Unfinished, on the record: repeatable regeneration (how much CO₂ actually comes back off the zeolite, at what concentration), compressor and buffer-tank integration, and controlled measurements of power and mass against those estimates. Next: build the regeneration stage for real, run controlled capture/release cycles with logged data, and replace the estimates above with measurements — even if the numbers get worse.

learnings.title: 🔍 Test Instead of Guess
learnings.text: When the motor driver would not respond, I stopped changing the main program and wrote a small I2C scanner. It found the board at 0x60. That changed how I debug problems: isolate one assumption, test it, then move on.

learnings.title: 🧩 Build the Whole System
learnings.text: The hardest part was not making one servo move. It was getting mechanics, electronics, firmware, Wi-Fi, and the browser interface to work together reliably.

question.heading: It started with a LEGO grabber that couldn't bend.
paragraphs: In sixth grade, I built a grabber out of LEGO. It could reach and grip, but it couldn't really bend. That bothered me more than it probably should have — years later I still wanted a better answer to that one small missing joint.
In between came the basics: a blinking LED to start, then sensors, an Arduino car, and a first web page that could control servos from my phone.

In 8th grade I came back to the original question — instead of only asking how to build something similar, I decided to build the whole system myself: the mechanics, the electronics, and the programming.

build.kicker: 02 · FROM A GRABBER TO AN ARM
build.heading: Building it: mechanics, mappings, and my own control system.
build.intro: Ashtavakra is not built from a kit or run by one. I connected the electronics, wrote the firmware, and built the interface it runs on.
paragraphs: The main controller is an Arduino UNO R4 WiFi, connected over I²C to an Emakefun Motor Driver V5.2 at address 0x60, which drives eight TD-8120MG servos — a six-degree-of-freedom arm plus a gripper, with one twin support servo on the lift.

The firmware is written in C++ for the parts that make it feel like one machine: per-servo offsets to fix horns that never sat perfectly straight, speed control, S-curve motion so joints glide instead of snap, a reset, and an emergency stop.
The browser controller is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It is the entire interface — no pre-built robotics app — and it talks to the UNO over Wi-Fi.

decision.heading: The Debugging Breakthrough
decision.key_heading: A small I²C scanner answered the question my whole program couldn't.
decision.intro: After a fried board, a missing I²C device, and strange servo channels, I stopped changing code until something worked and started collecting evidence instead.
paragraphs: When the motor driver went quiet, the answer was a small test, not more changes to the main program. I wrote a tiny I²C scanner — it found the board exactly where it was supposed to be, at address 0x60.

The same method caught the servo-horn misalignments too: one assumption at a time, then software offsets to calibrate each servo individually instead of repeatedly rebuilding the joints. Wire-by-wire checks along the way did the rest of the teaching.

items.title: Break problems into small tests
items.text: A tiny I²C scanner, one servo brought up alone, each channel and assumption checked separately — every tangle that stopped me was really three smaller problems stacked on top of each other.

items.title: Software can fix physical problems
items.text: Some servo horns were slightly misaligned. Instead of rebuilding the joints over and over, I added software offsets so each servo could be calibrated individually.

items.title: Build the whole system
items.text: The hardest part was not making one servo move. It was getting mechanics, electronics, firmware, Wi-Fi, and the browser interface to work together reliably.

items.title: A prototype is not the same animal as the vision
items.text: The arm that works today is still far from the arm I first imagined. Saying that out loud keeps the next steps honest — and the next steps real.

lessons.next_steps: Next: finish the Vision AI exploration, then keep exploring how the arm can do simple tasks with less help from me — one testable step at a time. In parallel, a clear bench photo of the arm goes on this page.

blog.page_subtitle: Build logs, debugging stories, and things I wish someone told me earlier. I write these because the gap between 'I want to build that' and 'I actually built that' is filled with mistakes most people never talk about.
index_intro: This is where I keep the build notes — the plans that broke, the fixes that worked, and the things I had to unlearn. Newest first. The fixes stay in the notes on purpose: most build stories stop at the result, and the interesting part is whatever was wrong with the first idea.
